triage.name: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
triage.reason: Weeks-old infant with progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting and a palpable olive; classic diagnosis from history, exam, electrolytes and ultrasound.

demographics: More common in males, with a male-to-female ratio of about 4:1
More common in White and Hispanic infants than in Black or Asian infants
Typically presents between 3 and 6 weeks of age, rarely after 3 months
family_history: Pyloric stenosis in a parent or sibling

chief_complaints.text: My baby vomits forcefully after every feed
The vomit shoots across the room
He is always hungry and wants to feed again right after vomiting

hpi.onset: Gradual, starting with occasional spitting up that becomes forceful over days to weeks
hpi.duration: Symptoms usually present for 1–3 weeks before diagnosis
hpi.progression: Vomiting becomes more frequent and forceful, eventually projectile after most feeds; the infant may begin to lose weight or fail to gain
hpi.location: Emesis is nonbilious; abdominal discomfort is not localized
hpi.quality: Forceful, projectile, nonbilious emesis after feeding
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; can lead to dehydration and weight loss
hpi.timing: Occurs shortly after feeding, typically within 30 minutes
relieving: Nothing consistently relieves it; the infant remains hungry and may feed again

associated_symptoms.text: Weight loss or poor weight gain

pertinent_negatives: Failure to pass meconium in the first 24 hours

atypical.how_it_differs: Preterm infants may present later and with less forceful vomiting; symptoms can be attributed to reflux or feeding intolerance.

general.mild: Alert, hungry, feeding well between episodes; no dehydration
general.moderate: Fussy, hungry but with some weight loss and mild dehydration
general.severe: Lethargic, sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, weight loss
general.critical: Lethargic or unresponsive, markedly dehydrated, shock

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen, especially the right upper quadrant, while the infant is calm or after a feeding
findings.finding: A firm, olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium
findings.term: Palpable mass in right upper quadrant

findings.maneuver: Observe the abdomen during or after a feeding
findings.finding: Visible waves of gastric peristalsis moving from left to right across the upper abdomen

findings.maneuver: Assess mucous membranes, skin turgor, fontanelle, and eyes
findings.finding: Dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, sunken fontanelle or eyes

findings.maneuver: Weigh the infant and compare with birth weight or previous weights
findings.finding: Weight loss or failure to gain weight

findings.maneuver: Observe or ask about the character of the vomitus

findings.finding: Abdomen not distended, soft, no tenderness or guarding

findings.maneuver: Ask about stool pattern and examine the diaper
findings.finding: Normal stools, no diarrhea or blood

findings.maneuver: Examine the inguinal and femoral regions for bulges

labs.caveat: Hypochloremia from loss of gastric hydrochloric acid in vomitus; the chloride falls before the sodium.
Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; the bicarbonate rises as hydrogen ions are lost in the vomitus.
Hypokalemia from renal potassium wasting driven by aldosterone in the setting of volume depletion and alkalosis.
Mild hyponatremia from vomiting and poor intake; usually less striking than the chloride or bicarbonate change.
Arterial or capillary blood gas; alkalemia confirms the metabolic alkalosis but is not needed for diagnosis.
Prerenal azotemia from dehydration and vomiting; falls with fluid resuscitation.
Infant reference ranges are lower than adult values; a rise from baseline suggests significant dehydration.
Concentrated urine from dehydration; supports volume depletion.
From poor intake and vomiting; not specific.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging in any infant with suspected pyloric stenosis

findings.text: Pyloric muscle thickness of 3 mm or more
Pyloric channel length of 15 mm or more
Elongated, thickened, echogenic pyloric muscle with a hypoechoic ring
Delayed or absent gastric emptying with a distended stomach
Nondiagnostic study when the pylorus is not clearly seen

imaging.preferred_when: When ultrasound is unavailable or nondiagnostic

findings.text: String sign: a thin, elongated stream of contrast through the narrowed pyloric channel
Double-track sign: two parallel streaks of contrast in the narrowed channel
Delayed gastric emptying with a distended stomach
Shoulder sign: indentation of the pyloric muscle on the gastric antrum
Usually nonspecific; may show a distended stomach with a paucity of distal bowel gas

initial.why: Detects the classic hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and guides fluid and electrolyte replacement
Baseline before surgery; helps exclude infection as a cause of vomiting
Confirms the diagnosis by measuring pyloric muscle thickness and channel length

supporting.why: Blood gas confirms the severity of the metabolic alkalosis when the bicarbonate is markedly elevated
Assesses hydration and ketosis; helps exclude a urinary infection
Alternative when ultrasound is unavailable or nondiagnostic

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management and does not show the pylorus
Radiation exposure with no added benefit over ultrasound in an infant
Not needed unless pancreatitis is suspected
Not routinely needed; vomiting is not primarily inflammatory

decision_points: Correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities before surgery; do not operate on an alkalotic, hypokalemic infant
Ultrasound is the first-line imaging study; reserve upper gastrointestinal series for nondiagnostic ultrasound
A palpable olive or classic ultrasound findings confirm the diagnosis without further imaging
Consider malrotation with volvulus if the vomitus is bilious or the infant is acutely ill

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux
differential.why_considered: Regurgitation and spitting up after feeds is extremely common in infants and is the usual first explanation for vomiting in this age group.

history: Effortless spitting up or regurgitation rather than forceful projectile emesis
Vomiting is not progressive and the infant is otherwise thriving
Symptoms often improve when held upright after feeds
exam: No palpable olive in the right upper quadrant
labs: Normal electrolytes; no hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
imaging: Pyloric muscle thickness and channel length are normal on ultrasound

differential.name: Malrotation with midgut volvulus
differential.why_considered: A congenital cause of intestinal obstruction in a young infant that can present with vomiting and must be recognized immediately because it is a surgical emergency.
differential.trigger: Bilious (green) vomiting or an acutely ill, lethargic infant with abdominal distension

history: Sudden onset of severe symptoms rather than gradual worsening over weeks
May have had episodes of feeding intolerance earlier
exam: Lethargy or signs of shock out of proportion to the vomiting history
labs: May show metabolic acidosis or shock physiology rather than hypochloremic alkalosis
imaging: Upper gastrointestinal series shows an abnormal duodenojejunal junction and a corkscrew appearance of the proximal small bowel
Ultrasound may show a whirlpool sign of twisted mesentery

differential.name: Adrenal hyperplasia (congenital adrenal hyperplasia with salt wasting)
differential.why_considered: A weeks-old infant with vomiting, poor feeding, weight loss and dehydration can have a metabolic crisis from salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
differential.trigger: Vomiting with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia or shock in a neonate

history: Poor feeding, lethargy and failure to thrive
Family history of ambiguous genitalia or neonatal death
exam: Ambiguous genitalia in a female infant or hyperpigmentation
labs: Metabolic acidosis rather than hypochloremic alkalosis

differential.name: Viral gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Vomiting in an infant is frequently infectious, especially with sick contacts or day-care exposure.

history: Vomiting is self-limited over days rather than progressive over weeks
exam: Diffuse abdominal tenderness without a mass
Signs of dehydration may be present but no olive
labs: Electrolytes may show dehydration but not the classic hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Infants with UTI can present with vomiting, poor feeding and irritability without localizing urinary symptoms.

history: Vomiting is not projectile or progressive
labs: Positive urinalysis with leukocyte esterase, nitrites and pyuria

differential.name: Increased intracranial pressure
differential.why_considered: Forceful vomiting in an infant can be a sign of raised intracranial pressure from hydrocephalus, hemorrhage or a mass.
differential.trigger: Vomiting with a bulging fontanelle, lethargy, seizures or abnormal head growth

history: Rapid head circumference growth or developmental regression
Vomiting may not be consistently related to feeds
exam: Bulging or tense fontanelle, separated sutures
Sunsetting eyes, cranial nerve palsies or abnormal tone
labs: Electrolytes are usually normal unless dehydration has developed
imaging: Head ultrasound, CT or MRI shows ventricular dilation or an intracranial lesion

severity.mild: Early disease: occasional nonbilious emesis that is becoming forceful, infant feeding well and gaining weight, no dehydration, normal or near-normal electrolytes
severity.moderate: Established disease: projectile nonbilious vomiting after most feeds, hungry infant, some weight loss and mild dehydration, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia
severity.severe: Advanced disease: persistent projectile vomiting, marked dehydration and weight loss, lethargy, significant hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
severity.critical: Decompensated disease: severe dehydration with shock, profound metabolic alkalosis, apnea or altered mental status; requires urgent resuscitation before surgery

red_flags.meaning: Suggests a more distal obstruction such as malrotation with midgut volvulus; a surgical emergency
Severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance; needs immediate resuscitation
Severe metabolic alkalosis or another critical cause; urgent evaluation and treatment
Suggests obstruction, volvulus or another surgical abdomen rather than uncomplicated pyloric stenosis

red_flags.finding: Failure to pass meconium in the first 24 hours or chronic constipation
red_flags.meaning: Points toward a distal obstruction or Hirschsprung disease rather than pyloric stenosis

complications.name: Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
clues: Lethargy or apnea in severe cases

complications.name: Failure to thrive and weight loss
clues: Poor weight gain or weight loss
Hungry infant who feeds but vomits

complications.name: Postoperative wound infection or dehiscence
clues: Fever, wound redness or discharge after pyloromyotomy

complications.name: Persistent postoperative vomiting
clues: Vomiting continuing for a few days after pyloromyotomy
Usually improves with small, frequent feeds

special_populations.differences: Preterm infants may present later and with less forceful vomiting; symptoms can be mistaken for reflux or feeding intolerance, and the classic olive may be harder to palpate.

key_questions.question: How old is your baby now, and when did the vomiting start?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset at 3–6 weeks of age; onset after 3 months makes pyloric stenosis unlikely

key_questions.question: Is the vomiting forceful or projectile, and how far does it travel?
key_questions.looking_for: Forceful, projectile emesis that may shoot several feet from the mouth

key_questions.question: What color is the vomit? Is it ever green or bloody?
key_questions.looking_for: Nonbilious, non-bloody; green (bilious) vomit points to a more distal obstruction such as malrotation with volvulus

key_questions.question: Does the vomiting happen right after feeding, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Occurs within about 30 minutes of most or all feeds and is becoming more frequent over days to weeks

key_questions.question: Is he still hungry and wanting to feed again right after vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Persistent hunger after vomiting; supports pyloric stenosis over an infectious or systemic cause

key_questions.question: Has he been gaining weight, or has he lost weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Weight loss or failure to gain weight; supports significant obstruction and dehydration

key_questions.question: How many wet diapers a day, and how many stools? Any diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Decreased urine output with constipation and no diarrhea; diarrhea suggests gastroenteritis

key_questions.question: Any fever, irritability, or lethargy?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and irritability suggest infection; lethargy suggests severe dehydration or a metabolic crisis

key_questions.question: Did he pass meconium in the first 24 hours, and has he had any abdominal distension?
key_questions.looking_for: Normal meconium passage and no distension; delayed meconium or distension suggests a distal obstruction or Hirschsprung disease

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of pyloric stenosis or of a baby needing surgery for vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Pyloric stenosis in a parent or sibling; increases risk

key_questions.question: Was he born preterm, and how has feeding been going overall?
key_questions.looking_for: Preterm infants may present later with less forceful vomiting that is mistaken for reflux or feeding intolerance

key_questions.question: Any sick contacts, day-care exposure, or recent travel?
key_questions.looking_for: Sick contacts suggest viral gastroenteritis rather than pyloric stenosis

reasoning_points: A weeks-old infant (typically 3–6 weeks) with progressive, forceful, nonbilious projectile vomiting after feeds
Persistent hunger after vomiting with weight loss or poor weight gain
A palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant or visible gastric peristaltic waves on exam
Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis on electrolytes from loss of gastric hydrochloric acid
Pyloric ultrasound showing muscle thickness of 3 mm or more and channel length of 15 mm or more
Bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, diarrhea, fever, or delayed meconium passage are absent and argue against other causes
Dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities are corrected before pyloromyotomy

easy: Male infant around 4–6 weeks of age
Classic story of projectile nonbilious vomiting after every feed
Palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant
Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis on the basic metabolic panel
medium: Vomiting described as 'spitting up' that is actually becoming forceful
No palpable olive; diagnosis rests on ultrasound
Mild dehydration with only borderline electrolyte changes
Female infant or an infant outside the classic 3–6 week window
Symptoms initially attributed to gastroesophageal reflux
hard: Preterm infant presenting later with less forceful vomiting and no olive
Infant with bilious vomiting or abdominal distension suggesting malrotation with volvulus instead
Neonate with vomiting, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and shock suggesting salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Infant with fever and irritability suggesting urinary tract infection or gastroenteritis
Severe dehydration with profound metabolic alkalosis and lethargy at presentation
